How AI detectors work

AI detectors can look like magic or like guesswork. They are neither. Here is what happens between pasting a text and seeing a percentage.

Published 17 November 2026

The basic idea

A language model writes by choosing, again and again, a likely next word. That leaves a statistical fingerprint: the text is smoother and more predictable than most people’s writing. Detectors look for that fingerprint. They do not compare your text with a database of AI output, and they cannot trace it back to a particular chatbot session.

Three families of detector

  • Statistical detectors run the text through a language model and measure how predictable it is, a quantity called perplexity, and how much that predictability varies from sentence to sentence. Low, even perplexity suggests machine text.
  • Trained classifiers are models taught on large sets of labelled human and AI passages. They learn their own features. They can be accurate on text like their training data and unreliable on anything different, such as a new model’s output, another language, or an unusual genre.
  • Rule-based detectors measure visible style features directly: stock phrases, even sentence lengths, formulaic openers, tidy lists of three, the absence of a personal voice. They are transparent and need no model, but they are the easiest to fool and the most likely to misjudge formal writing. The detector on this site is of this kind, and says so.

Why no detector is certain

Human and machine writing overlap. Some people write smoothly and evenly; a model can be prompted to write unevenly. Light editing of AI text, or translating it, changes the statistics a detector depends on. Every detector therefore makes two kinds of error: it flags some human writing as AI, and it passes some AI writing as human. Reducing one kind of error increases the other.

How to read a score

A score of 80 does not mean “80 percent of this was written by AI”, and it does not mean “there is an 80 percent chance this is AI”. It means the text sits toward the machine-like end of whatever that detector measures. Three questions make a score more useful:

  • How much text was there? Under about a hundred words, treat any result as weak.
  • What kind of text is it? Formal, technical and second-language writing score higher on most detectors.
  • What does the detector say about itself? Prefer tools that state a confidence level, show which sentences drove the result, and publish how they were tested.
